title: The rational identity matrix is a right unit for matrix multiplication, on its range
statement: For a matrix A over the constructed rationals (a function Nat -> Nat -> Rat), a dimension n, and indices i and j WITH j < n, the (i, j) entry of A * matId equals A i j. The bound is on the COLUMN index j here, where the left unit law (F:rat-matmul-id-left) bounds the row index i: the summation runs over the shared inner index, so which of the two outer indices has to lie in range depends on which side the identity sits. Stated pointwise; `funext` is absent from this kernel so an Eq between matrices is not available.

formal.statement: theorem Rat.matMul_id_right : ((x0 : ((x0 : AxNat) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> Rat))) -> ((x1 : AxNat) -> ((x2 : AxNat) -> ((x3 : AxNat) -> ((x4 : AxNat.lt x3 x1) -> Eq.{1} Rat (Rat.matMul x0 Rat.matId x1 x2 x3) (x0 x2 x3))))))

evidence.supports: Rat.matMul_id_right is admitted by the trusted kernel gate with the type recorded in formal.statement. It shares Rat.sumRange_delta with the left unit law and is the shorter of the two: the delta's hypothesis wants `t != j`, which is exactly the shape Rat.matId_off_diag takes on this side, so no ne_symm is needed and the tail closes with mul_one without a mul_comm.

notes: WHAT IS NOT PROVED. The two unit laws together do NOT give a monoid structure on matrices in any type-theoretic sense: there is no carrier of `n x n` matrices, no Eq on it, and no closure statement. What exists is a product operation, an associativity law and two unit laws, all pointwise, over the encoding `Nat -> Nat -> Rat` with dimensions as ordinary arguments. Nor is there an inverse for any matrix.
